scenes.narration: Apple is worth about five point oh six trillion dollars. That is the price of every share, three hundred and forty-eight dollars and fifty-one cents at the close on November tenth, twenty twenty-six, times about fourteen and a half billion shares. By our math, that is about thirty-eight times last year's profit.
And here's the twist. The thing everyone pictures, the iPhone, brings in more than half the money. But the part that quietly makes the most profit per dollar is something you never hold in your hand.
So what is that price actually betting on? What has to happen for it to keep working? And what could break it?
In the next few minutes, we open the machine, follow the cash, run the numbers on what's priced in, and finish with the three numbers to watch when Apple reports next.
Quick note. This isn't financial advice. Everything here comes from Apple's own filings and our own math, dated, so you can decide for yourself.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: In fiscal twenty twenty-six, Apple sold about four hundred and seventy-nine billion dollars of stuff, up fifteen percent, after just six percent the year before. The iPhone alone was about two hundred and fifty-four billion dollars, up twenty-one percent, and fifty-three percent of everything. Mac, iPad and the wearables pipe are smaller, and iPad and wearables were basically flat.

Then there's the pipe you can't see. Services, meaning the App Store, cloud, advertising, payments and subscriptions, brought in about one hundred and twenty-three billion dollars, about a quarter of sales. But its gross margin was seventy-six percent, against thirty-nine percent for the hardware. So Services makes forty percent of Apple's gross profit. A quarter of the revenue, two fifths of the profit.

Where does it come from? Greater China came roaring back, about eighty-two billion dollars, up twenty-eight percent, after falling four percent the year before. About about sixty percent of sales go through carriers, retailers and resellers, not Apple's own stores. And almost all the hardware is built by partners across Asia, from China mainland and India to Vietnam. So Apple owns the brand, the software and the customer, while other companies run most of the factories.

Apple's year also has a very uneven rhythm. The December quarter alone brought in about one hundred and forty-four billion dollars, about thirty percent of the whole year, with about eighty-five billion dollars from the iPhone in just those three months. Now look at the September quarter, the one just reported. The iPhone grew seventeen and a half percent and the Mac almost twenty-four percent, while the iPad fell about ten percent and wearables slipped about eight percent. So two product lines carried the growth, and two of them shrank.

Let me draw the machine. Here are the products, the big pipe, with a thinner margin. Here is Services, the smaller pipe, with a fat margin. Both pour into gross profit. And this arrow is the one investors watch, because every point of Services growth carries far more profit than a point of hardware.

scenes.narration: A machine that profitable throws off a lot of cash. So where does the cash go?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Operating cash flow was one hundred and forty-five billion dollars. Capital spending was only about nine billion dollars, about six percent of that. So free cash flow, by our math, was one hundred and thirty-six billion dollars. That's more than net income, which was one hundred and thirty-two billion dollars.

And Apple hands most of it back. It bought back eighty-five point eight billion dollars of its own shares, and paid about sixteen billion dollars in dividends. Together, about seventy-five percent of free cash flow, by our math. The share count has dropped by about seven percent since mid twenty twenty-three, so each remaining share owns a slightly bigger slice. That's a quiet tailwind for earnings per share, even in a year when total profit stands still.

One caveat. Apple's low capital spending does not mean artificial intelligence is free. Research and development jumped thirty-two percent to about forty-six billion dollars, mainly because of infrastructure costs, including A I. And Apple says it relies on third party cloud providers for compute. So part of the A I bill shows up as an expense, not as capex.

Now, one honest footnote on all that cash. Operating cash flow jumped from about one hundred and eleven billion dollars to one hundred and forty-five billion dollars, about thirty percent in a single year. Part of that was timing. A swing in other liabilities added about fourteen billion dollars this year, after taking away about eleven billion dollars the year before. And inventories climbed from about six billion dollars to about fourteen and a half billion dollars. So this year's cash was strong, but not all of it is a new normal. And the day before our data date, Apple still sold seven and a half billion dollars of new bonds, even with net cash of about fifty-seven billion dollars.

Let me draw where a year of free cash went. Here is the free cash flow bar. Here is the buyback bar, by far the biggest. Here are the dividends. And this small piece is what was left over. Most of the money goes straight back to shareholders.

scenes.narration: Which brings us to the big question. At five trillion dollars, what are you paying for?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Three quick lenses first, all our math on the latest fiscal year. Price to earnings, about thirty-eight times. Free cash flow yield, about two point seven percent. Operating cash flow yield, about two point nine percent. Apple has net cash of about fifty-seven billion dollars, which barely moves a number this size. And because its capex is small and steady, free cash flow is a fair base here.

Now let's run it backwards. We ask what growth in free cash flow, for the next ten years, makes today's price work, then assume growth slows to three percent forever. With an eight percent discount rate, the answer is about ten and a half percent a year. With ten percent, it's about fifteen and a half percent. Our illustration, with the assumptions on screen.

For contrast, if free cash flow simply stayed flat forever, the same model gives a company worth about two point two trillion dollars at eight percent, or about one point six trillion dollars at ten. So more than half of today's price is a bet on growth.

Let me draw that gap. Here is what flat cash would be worth at ten percent. Here it is at eight. And here is the actual price, towering over both. That gap is the growth the market is paying for in advance.

scenes.narration: Is that growth unusual for Apple? Last year, sales grew fifteen percent. The year before, six percent. So the price assumes the strong year was not a one off, at least at the lower discount rate, and something even better at the higher one.

scenes.narration: Number one, the iPhone keeps compounding from a record. It just grew twenty-one percent to about two hundred and fifty-four billion dollars. Beating that every year means people keep upgrading, and Apple keeps getting enough chips and memory to build them. A record year is great news, and also a harder bar to clear next time.

Number two, Services keeps growing fast. It's the profit engine, but its growth slowed to nine point eight percent in the September quarter, the slowest of the year. If that line keeps cooling, the whole growth story gets harder.

Number three, margins hold. The September quarter's gross margin was forty-seven point nine percent, and that included about one point from tariff refunds that may not come back. Apple itself warns of downward pressure, and says memory and storage costs are rising, and expected to rise further.

And number four, China keeps buying. That rebound to about eighty-two billion dollars did a lot of the heavy lifting last year. One weak year there would show up fast, because the region is more than a sixth of Apple's sales, and it swung from shrinking to booming in a single year.

scenes.narration: Now the other side of the scale.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Risk one is the courts. Apple earns licensing money from Google for search, and says that if the antitrust ruling against Google is reversed on appeal, remedies could block those payments. Apple doesn't say how much is at stake. The App Store fight with Epic is now headed to the Supreme Court. And the Justice Department's antitrust suit is still going.

Risk two is Europe. Under the Digital Markets Act, Apple was already fined in twenty twenty-five, and is appealing. In the open investigation, the law allows fines of up to ten percent of worldwide sales. On last year's sales, that ceiling would be about forty-eight billion dollars. That's a legal maximum, not an estimate.

Risk three is everything Apple doesn't control. Tariffs can still hit costs. Memory prices are climbing. And on artificial intelligence, Apple warns that failing to keep up with rivals could cost it market share.

And there's a quieter concentration risk. Almost all of Apple's hardware is built by outsourcing partners, and just two suppliers account for forty-five percent and twenty-seven percent of the money vendors owe Apple. On the selling side, phone carriers make up a third of what customers owe Apple, and one single customer alone is thirteen percent. Apple doesn't name any of them. But if one big partner stumbles, on either end of the chain, it shows up in Apple's numbers.

And the upside the price might not fully include. Apple says its installed base of active devices hit a new all-time high, in every major category and region, though it gives no number. New cloud services will expand access to its A I features, with no pricing announced yet. And advertising is already one of the lines driving Services. None of that is sized, so we won't size it either.

scenes.narration: So, what should you watch?

Here's the scorecard for the next report, expected around late January twenty twenty-seven, our estimate. One, December quarter revenue against about one hundred and forty-four billion dollars a year earlier. Two, gross margin against forty-seven point nine percent, which still had tariff refunds in it. Three, Services growth against nine point eight percent. If those three hold up, the story the price is telling keeps holding up. If they crack, the gap between the price and the cash gets harder to defend.
That's Apple, November twenty twenty-six edition. We'll update it after every report, with new numbers and the same three questions. What's priced in, what has to happen, and what could go wrong.
